title: Interface Segregation Principle
summary: Many small, client-specific interfaces beat one fat interface that forces implementers to support methods they don't need.

slides.markdown:
The **Interface Segregation Principle** (ISP) says clients shouldn't be forced to depend on methods they don't use. Instead of one large interface covering every possible operation, prefer several small, focused ones.

Think of a Swiss Army knife handed to a chef: they only need the blade, but they're stuck carrying the scissors, corkscrew, and toothpick anyway. ISP is about not handing out more surface area than a caller actually needs.

slides.sectionTitle: ISP defined: many small client-specific interfaces over one fat interface
slides.markdown:
ISP says: **no client should be forced to depend on methods it doesn't use.** Where SRP is about a class having one reason to change, ISP is about an interface not forcing an implementer — or a caller — to deal with capabilities irrelevant to them.

A `Worker` interface with `work()`, `eat()`, and `sleep()` forces every implementer to provide all three, even ones for whom one or two make no sense. Splitting into `Workable`, `Eatable`, and `Sleepable` lets each class implement only what actually applies to it.

slides.sectionTitle: The "fat interface" smell: forced no-op/throwing implementations
slides.markdown:
The clearest sign of a fat interface is an implementation that can't honestly fulfill part of the contract. It either does nothing (`void eat() {}` — silently lying that it worked) or throws (`void eat() { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }` — a runtime surprise for any caller who assumed the interface's promise held).

Both are symptoms, not fixes — they're the code admitting the interface asked for more than this implementer can honestly provide. The real fix is splitting the interface so implementers only sign up for capabilities they actually have.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: one bloated interface split into role interfaces
slides.markdown:

Splitting into role interfaces means `Robot` simply never implements `Eatable` or `Sleepable` — there's no forced no-op method to write or maintain, and no caller can accidentally call an operation that was never real for that type.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a Worker interface forcing a Robot to implement eat()
Compare: ISP vs SRP — segregating interfaces vs segregating responsibilities
slides.markdown:
ISP and SRP are frequently confused because both push toward "smaller, more focused units" — but they operate on different things:

| | SRP | ISP |
|---|---|---|
| Applies to | Classes (implementations) | Interfaces (contracts) |
| Question it asks | "How many reasons does this class have to change?" | "Is this caller forced to depend on methods it doesn't use?" |
| Violation looks like | A class mixing pricing, persistence, and formatting | One interface with `work()`, `eat()`, `sleep()` forcing irrelevant methods on some implementers |
| Fix | Split the class into collaborators | Split the interface into role-specific interfaces |

**How to decide which applies:** if the pain is "this class does too much," it's SRP; if the pain is "this contract makes me implement things I don't need," it's ISP. A single design often benefits from both fixes at once.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: interface explosion — too many micro-interfaces to track
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "ISP means every method should live in its own single-method interface, so smaller is always better."

**Why it's wrong:** splitting past the point where methods are genuinely used by different clients creates dozens of micro-interfaces that always get implemented together anyway — now every class declaration is a long `implements` list, and finding "what can this type actually do" means hunting across ten files instead of one.

**Correct model:** group methods by **who actually uses them together**. If every real caller of `Eatable` also always needs `Sleepable`, they were never separate client needs — merge them. Segregate along real usage boundaries, not for the sake of smallness.

slides.sectionTitle: How ISP guides API design for consumers you don't control
slides.markdown:
ISP matters most when you're shipping an interface to consumers you can't coordinate with — a public SDK, an internal platform team's API, a plugin contract. You can't ask every downstream team what they need before they need it, so a fat interface becomes a permanent tax: every consumer pays the cost of methods they never call, and every future implementer has to fake support for capabilities irrelevant to them.

A practical rule for public APIs: design the smallest interface that satisfies the *most common* single use case, and let consumers who need more compose additional small interfaces — don't hand everyone the maximal contract by default.
